blocks.text: The structure and chemical composition of chromosomes differ in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; this section deals with chromosomes in eukaryotic cells.

Chromosomes are thin, thread-like structures made of DNA and histone proteins. Their number and shape differ in each species, and the complete set is the karyotype. In the body (somatic) cells of diploid organisms chromosomes occur in pairs, the homologous chromosomes; gametes have half the number, not in pairs.

When a cell is not dividing (interphase) its chromosomes are not visible as separate structures: they stay uncoiled as a fine network called chromatin. As the cell prepares to divide, the DNA coils round small units of histones, these units coil further, and with more coiling and condensation the structure becomes thicker and shorter, finally forming compact thread-like chromosomes.

blocks.prompt: What is chromatin, and when do chromosomes become visible?
blocks.explanation: Chromatin is the fine, uncoiled network of DNA and histones in a non-dividing (interphase) nucleus. Chromosomes become visible when the cell prepares to divide and the chromatin coils and condenses.

items: Chromosomes: DNA + histones; the full set is the karyotype.
Somatic cells: homologous pairs; gametes: half the number.
Interphase: chromatin; division: coiled, condensed chromosomes.
